title: PAYG credit decay model — scratch
body:
Purpose / quick summary:

This is a rough scratchpad exploring a PAYG credit system that decays (or 'evaporates') over time instead of a hard expiration. Goal: give new users tail-room to experiment without creating long-term liability/abuse surface. Fit for free-credit trials, onboarding bonuses, and occasional promotional credits.

Key requirements / constraints (informal):
- Credits should be simple for users to understand (but we can have internal details).
- Minimize balance hoarding (people stacking credits forever).
- Limit arbitrage/abuse where folks repeatedly create accounts to farm short-lived promos.
- Accounting-friendly: predictable monthly liability estimate.
- Integrates with existing token-based billing (we measure usage in delta-tokens consumed per request).

Assumptions (back-of-envelope baseline numbers — change them easily):
- Infra cost: $0.80 per 1M input+output tokens (weighted average across model mix and batching) — this is our internal marginal cost assumption for now.
- Retail-like list price we expose: $1.50 per 1M tokens (i.e., ~1.875x markup over infra in this scenario).
- Typical new user: 1–10k tokens/day while exploring.
- Promo credit pool examples: $10, $25, $50 credits applied to account.

Design idea: continuous exponential decay + floor eviction
- Credits are represented as USD-equivalent (not token-equivalent) to keep it simple.
- Each credit grant has: amount, grant_ts, decay_rate (lambda), optional max-lifetime.
- Effective_available_credit(t) = sum_i amount_i * exp(-lambda * (t - grant_ts))
- Practical implementation: discrete daily decay (apply factor daily) for simpler ledger ops.
- Decay rate choice controls half-life: half_life_days = ln(2) / lambda.

Why decay vs hard expiry?
- Hard expiry causes churn/complaints when a user loses promo they were saving for a project.
- Decay reduces liability gradually, is friendlier, and still disincentivizes hoarding.
- It also allows us to nudge usage behavior via announcements (e.g., "your credit decays 5%/week").

Sample parameterizations (pick one):
A) Fast decay (aggressive anti-hoard): half-life = 14 days (~5% daily decay)
B) Medium decay (balanced): half-life = 60 days (~1.14% daily decay)
C) Slow decay (marketing-friendly): half-life = 180 days (~0.385% daily decay)
D) Hybrid: initial grace period (30 days no decay) then medium decay thereafter

Daily decay factor formula (discrete): factor = 2^(-1 / half_life_days)  (i.e., daily multiplier)
- Example numeric factors: 14d -> ~0.953/day, 60d -> ~0.9886/day, 180d -> ~0.9962/day

Token math integration (USD credits -> tokens):
- At time of use, we convert request tokens to USD cost using the listed price (not infra cost) so user-visible balances match expectations.
- e.g., user request uses 4,800 tokens; listed price = $1.50 / 1M -> request cost = 4800 * (1.5 / 1,000,000) = $0.0072. Deduct from decayed credit.

Back-of-envelope scenarios (using medium decay / 60d half-life, factor ~0.9886/day):
- Promo: $25 grant on Day 0. Balance schedule (rounded):
  Day 0: 25.00
  Day 7: 25 * 0.9886^7 ≈ 23.47 (~6% lost)
  Day 30: ≈ 20.03 (~20% lost)
  Day 90: ≈ 12.28 (~51% lost)

User behavior examples:
1) Light explorer: 3k tokens/day -> daily USD cost = 3000*(1.5/1e6)= $0.0045/day.
   $25 covers ~25/0.0045 ≈ 5,555 days (~15 years) if no decay. With decay, it's used faster but still generous: because decay removes credit even if idle, the effective horizon is shorter.
   Simulation approx: we can compute time_to_deplete solving integral, but for scratch: after 60 days you have ~20 USD left; net consumption over first 60d from usage is ~0.27 USD (negligible), so decay dominates for very light users. This achieves anti-hoarding.

2) Active experimenter: 50k tokens/day -> $0.075/day. A $25 grant covers ~333 days if no decay. With medium decay, user will likely burn credits before decay becomes the main sink.

3) Burst user: runs a big job: 1.5M tokens job -> cost = 1.5M*(1.5/1e6) = $2.25. A single burst can consume large promos quickly — intended.

Liability estimation model (finance view):
- For N grants in period, expected outstanding liability next month = sum(amount_i * exp(-lambda * dt_i)) minus expected redemptions. But we should be conservative and assume a fraction of users will redeem early.
- Empirical approach: track cohort burn curves (grant day -> daily spend) and fit decay+usage parameters.

Abuse vectors & mitigations: 
- Create-account -> use quick heavy burst -> abandon (still consumes credits but cost to us grows). Mitigation: require phone/email verification for promo eligibility, limit first-24h max tokens/day for new accounts with credits, or reduce credit value for first 7 days.
- Account churn farming: since decay reduces value over time, farming loses effectiveness; still need fraud detection (behavioral, IP/phone heuristics).
- Credit arbitrage across regions/pricing tiers: credits are USD-equivalent and should always be priced at the account region price to reduce arbitrage.

Edge cases / implementation notes (ops):
- Ledger model: store grants as separate rows, compute daily decay tick job that writes new "available" number or simply compute on read. For billing and audits a daily snapshot is nicer.
- Refunds / chargebacks: if a paid invoice leads to refund, how do credits interact? Simpler: credits from refunds only apply if invoice paid created credits; or never auto-add credits on refunds. TODO decide.
- Rounding: compute USD at request-level seconds with microcents? Simpler to keep 4 decimal places for USD credit and round at cent for billing export.

Sensitivity mini-table (how many restless users before it costs us X):
- If average new-account consumes 10k tokens in first 7 days (~$0.015), decay dominates on small promo values. So $10 promo with 60d half-life mostly evaporates unless user is active. Good for anti-hoard.
- If infra cost is actually $0.40/M tokens instead of $0.80, our promotion becomes 2x cheaper — we should recalc in modeling layer. Keep a single param file for infra_cost and list_price so spreadsheets can repro.

Examples of simple rules to combine with decay (to enforce fairness):
- Cap daily redemption while credits active: first 7 days capped at 200k tokens/day. (prevents quick-siphon).
- If credits > X and account age < 3 days => require 2FA or phone.
- Promotional credits are flagged (metadata) and excluded from certain partner/affiliate payouts.

Open questions / TODOs (quick list):
- Do we communicate half-life clearly in UI? "Your credits decay at 1.14% per day (60d half-life)" feels too math-y. Maybe: "Credit value halves every ~2 months" - test with UX.
- Does marketing want short hard-expiry promos for urgency? Keep both options: decay + optional hard-expiry override.
- Exact decay implementation: continuous math (more accurate) or daily tick (simpler)? Go daily tick for ledger simplicity.
- Accounting: confirm with finance how to report remaining promo liability. They may want daily snapshots for MRR reconciliation.
- Security: add abuse heuristics to promo grant flow.

Quick experiments to run (notes for later):
- Simulate cohorts: create Monte Carlo sim with: user-type distributions (light/med/heavy), grant sizes ($10/$25/$50), decay half-lives (14/60/180) and infra costs (0.4/0.8). Output expected cost per grant.
- A/B test: medium decay vs hybrid (30d grace then decay) on new signup activation and long-term retention. Metric: % convert to paid within 90d, cost per converted user.

Random scribbles / heuristics:
- If promo goal is "drive quick conversion" use slower decay/higher immediate value; if goal is "prevent hoard and give sampling" use faster decay.
- We can combo: give small non-decaying credit for immediate trials ($1) + decaying larger credit for longer-term nudges ($20 decays). Low-friction immediate trial keeps UX happy while decay prevents hoard.

Notes to self: link the simulation code to PRJ-4321; ask Michael for the infra_cost time series he used in last month deck (ticket PRJ-3956).

End of scratch — lots to tidy before putting into product spec.
